Affright
af-FRITE
verb
From the Saxon afyrhtan, to terrify — the intensive prefix with fright. To strike with sudden and overpowering fear, stronger than to alarm and more sudden than to dread.

Biblical Definition

Affright is terror used as a weapon, and its chief biblical instance shows exactly how the enemy of God’s people fights. Sennacherib’s officers stood beneath the wall of Jerusalem and “cried with a loud voice in the Jews’ speech unto the people of Jerusalem that were on the wall, to affright them, and to trouble them; that they might take the city” (2Ch 32:18). Mark the strategy. They shouted in Hebrew, not Assyrian, so that the common people on the wall would understand and lose heart. The object was stated plainly: that they might take the city. Terror was the siege engine; the walls were to be brought down from the inside, by the fears of the men standing on them. That is still the method. The adversary speaks in a language the saints understand, aims at the defenders rather than the defences, and seeks to win by fear what he cannot win by force. Scripture’s answer is not that the danger is imaginary — Sennacherib was a real king with a real army — but that the LORD is greater: with him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God to help us, and to fight our battles. The word appears elsewhere of men astonished at the ruin of the wicked (Job 18:20), where the terror is not a weapon but a warning.

Webster 1828 Definition

To impress with sudden fear; to terrify. In Scripture, chiefly the enemy’s deliberate use of terror as a means of conquest.

AFFRIGHT, v.t. To impress with sudden fear; to frighten; to terrify or alarm.

From the Saxon afyrhtan, to terrify; the prefix intensive.

Stronger than alarm, which may be momentary; affright overpowers.

Used of terror employed as a stratagem of war (2Ch 32:18).

In the passive, to be struck with astonishment at a judgment (Job 18:20).

Key Scripture

2Ch 32:18 — "Then they cried with a loud voice in the Jews' speech unto the people of Jerusalem that were on the wall, to affright them, and to trouble them; that they might take the city."

Job 18:20 — "They that come after him shall be astonied at his day, as they that went before were affrighted ."

2Ch 32:7 — "Be strong and courageous, be not afraid nor dismayed for the king of Assyria, nor for all the multitude that is with him: for there be more with us than with him:"

2Ch 32:8 — "With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God to help us, and to fight our battles. And the people rested themselves upon the words of Hezekiah king of Judah."

Modern Corruption

Fear is now marketed continuously as a means of managing populations and selling remedies, which is precisely the Rabshakeh’s method — terror aimed at the defenders in a language they understand.

expand to see more

The corruption is the industrial use of dread. Whole trades now depend upon keeping people affrighted: the endless cycle of alarm that sells news, the crisis that must never be allowed to pass, the appeal that opens by describing a catastrophe and closes by naming its price. The technique is old enough to be described in 2Ch 32. Speak in the people’s own tongue; address the ordinary men on the wall rather than the king in his palace; magnify the enemy; and above all suggest that their God cannot deliver them. Hezekiah’s answer is the model of a right response — he neither denied the Assyrian army nor conceded its conclusion, but set the arm of flesh against the LORD our God, and then went and spread the letter before the LORD.

Recover the plain sense: the Christian is not promised freedom from danger but is forbidden the paralysis that danger aims to produce. Be strong and courageous, be not afraid nor dismayed for the king of Assyria was said while the king of Assyria was actually at the gate. Fear of God is the appointed cure for the fear of man, because a soul genuinely afraid of the Almighty has very little capacity left for being affrighted by anyone else. The Rabshakeh took no city that day. The angel of the LORD went out, and the great king went home with shame of face.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon afyrhtan, to terrify — sudden overwhelming fear, used by the enemy as a siege weapon against the defenders’ hearts.

expand to see more

Affright — Saxon afyrhtan, to terrify; intensive of fright.

Stronger and more sudden than alarm or dread.

2Ch 32:18: terror deliberately employed that they might take the city.

The Rabshakeh spoke in the Jews’ speech so the common people would understand.

Job 18:20: men affrighted at the day of the wicked — terror as warning, not weapon.

Usage

"2Ch 32:18 states the aim of terror outright: to take the city by the fears of its defenders."

"Hezekiah answers not by denying the danger but by naming a greater help (2Ch 32:8)."

"The fear of God is the appointed antidote to the fear of man."
